ch47.anchor: the historical place of Ashikaga Takauji
ch47.note: Ashikaga Takauji (1305–1358) founded the Muromachi shogunate after breaking with Emperor Go-Daigo and setting up a rival “Northern” emperor, driving Go-Daigo’s “Southern Court” into exile. The Mito school of history — whose monument was the vast Dai Nihon-shi begun under Tokugawa Mitsukuni (1628–1701) — treated the Southern Court as the legitimate line, and so branded Takauji the arch-traitor and exalted his enemy Kusunoki Masashige (see chapter 6), who died for Go-Daigo, as the model loyal subject. By the 1860s this framing was the shared assumption of educated men on every side; it is the exact fear driving the passage — Yoshinobu would sooner desert his army than fight the Emperor’s banner and go down in history as “a second Takauji.” The account here is accurate to how the period understood itself.

ch47.anchor: the newly-appointed infantry captain Matsudaira Tarō
ch47.note: Matsudaira Tarō (1839–1909), a Western-minded shogunal official who would follow Enomoto Takeaki north and become vice-president of the short-lived Ezo republic at Hakodate — the campaign this novel is moving toward, and the “fate” the narrator foreshadows here. He appeared in the previous chapter as the friend who first told Fukuchi of Yoshinobu’s flight.

The Hohei kokoro-e (“Infantry Handbook”), a translation of a Dutch army drill-book of 1860, issued by the shogunate’s military institute. The technical vocabulary Toshizō sounds out — soldaat (private), compagnie (company), onderofficier (non-commissioned officer), korporaal (corporal) — is Dutch, the language through which the shogunate first took in Western military science before the switch to French instruction. That Toshizō, an unlettered farmer’s son, reads a foreign drill-manual with delight while high officials dither is the chapter’s quiet point.

The Fujiyama (Fujisan) was an American-built steam warship of the shogunal navy, among the more modern vessels in Japanese waters. It carried the Osaka remnant, the Shinsengumi included, back to Edo after the collapse at Toba-Fushimi.

In the old twelve-fold reckoning of the day, the Hour of the Ox (ushi no koku) ran roughly from one to three in the morning — the dead of night, chosen here so the corps could slip out of Osaka unobserved.

ch47.anchor: a crested formal coat and Sendai-hira hakama
ch47.note: Toshizō dresses for Oyuki in his best: a montsuki, the black silk coat bearing the family crest worn on formal occasions, over hakama of Sendai-hira, a fine ribbed silk from Sendai long prized as the finest cloth for a man’s formal trousers. For the blunt soldier of the preceding chapters to take such care is the measure of the meeting.
